rationales.A: The New Deal protected unions in the Wagner Act and set labor standards in 1938. It did not ignore labor.
rationales.B: The problem Hine photographed in 1911 got its federal answer in 1938. Background: the Fair Labor Standards Act set a federal minimum wage and restricted child labor, carrying the Progressive impulse into New Deal law.
rationales.C: The Court struck down the NIRA in 1935, but the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 survived. Federal labor regulation was not banned permanently.
rationales.D: Domestic reform returned in force in the 1930s. Foreign policy did not replace it.
rationales.general:
1. Fix the starting point. In 1911 the reformers’ problem was children working in factories and canneries.
2. Follow the impulse forward. The Progressive push for labor laws did not die in the 1920s; it waited for a crisis.
3. Land in the New Deal. The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 set a minimum wage and restricted child labor nationwide.
4. Name the pattern. One impulse, two generations: Progressive exposure first, federal law second.
Remember: tracing an idea across a period means finding its later form, not only its first appearance.
